lesson.title: Water's Stubborn Temperature: Understanding Specific Heat Capacity
lesson.summary: Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius, and it explains why identical amounts of heat produce very different temperature changes in different materials.
lesson.body:
Drop a hot piece of aluminum foil and a hot ceramic mug on the counter and, even if they started at the same temperature and have the same mass, they will not cool at the same rate or feel the same to the touch. That difference comes down to specific heat capacity, symbolized c, defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of exactly one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius. Its units are joules per gram per degree Celsius, J/(g times degree C). Specific heat capacity is an intensive property, meaning it does not depend on how much of the substance you have. A gram of water and a swimming pool full of water share the same specific heat capacity, even though the pool obviously requires far more total energy to heat.

Why do substances differ so much in this property? It comes down to what is happening at the level of matter itself: how the particles are bonded and how many ways they have of storing energy. Water molecules form extensive hydrogen bonds with their neighbors, and heating water means fighting against and reorganizing that whole network, which soaks up a large amount of energy before the temperature actually rises. Metals, in contrast, are held together by a sea of loosely bound electrons around fixed metal cations, a structure that lets kinetic energy raise the temperature much more easily. This is why water has one of the highest specific heat capacities of any common substance, about 4.18 J/(g times degree C), while metals typically sit below 1 J/(g times degree C).

The defining equation is q = m c delta T, where q is the heat absorbed or released in joules, m is the mass in grams, c is the specific heat capacity, and delta T is the final temperature minus the initial temperature. If delta T is positive (the object warms up), q comes out positive, meaning heat was absorbed. If delta T is negative (the object cools down), q comes out negative, meaning heat was released. This equation is the single most used tool in this unit, so it is worth memorizing exactly.

Consider a 250.0 g block of aluminum, c = 0.897 J/(g times degree C), heated from 25.0 degrees C to 55.0 degrees C. The temperature change is delta T = 55.0 minus 25.0 = 30.0 degrees C. Then q = (250.0 g)(0.897 J/(g times degree C))(30.0 degrees C). First, 250.0 times 0.897 equals 224.25 J per degree C. Multiplying by 30.0 degrees C gives 6,727.5 J, or 6.73 kJ. Now compare that to heating the same mass of water through the same temperature change: q = (250.0 g)(4.18 J/(g times degree C))(30.0 degrees C). Here 250.0 times 4.18 equals 1,045 J per degree C, and multiplying by 30.0 degrees C gives 31,350 J, or 31.4 kJ, roughly four and a half times more energy than the aluminum needed for the identical mass and temperature change. That single comparison explains why oceans and large lakes moderate the climate of nearby land, why water is used as a coolant in engines and nuclear reactors, and why a metal pan handle heats up dangerously fast while the water inside stays cool much longer.
